title: AI 研究者讨论递归自我改进究竟有多近
author: Dwarkesh Patel
content:
Brief Description

Dwarkesh Patel convenes Beren Millidge of Zyphra, John Schulman of Thinking Machines, and Charlie O’Neill of Baseten to debate recursive self-improvement in AI. They examine whether present-day scaling and reinforcement learning can yield systems that accelerate AI research, what could prevent that outcome, the limits of simulated environments and online learning, and how soon AI might become a capable remote worker or exceed humans across computer-based cognitive work.

Table of Contents

  • The case for a slow or non-transformative future
  • Recursive self-improvement and research bottlenecks
  • Generalization, objectives, and scientific discovery
  • Environments, domain training, and learning from deployment
  • Data, architecture, parameters, and scaling laws
  • Forecasts for remote work, research acceleration, and ASI

The case for a slow or non-transformative future

Dwarkesh Patel: The opening question asks why, absent war, bans, or other political shocks, the world might reach the mid-2030s without billions of superintelligent systems radically transforming it. Beren Millidge suggests a persistent gap between benchmark or simulation performance and consequential real-world performance. Systems could become extremely good at tasks people specify while remaining unable to transfer that competence broadly enough, particularly if meta-learning and continual learning remain difficult.

John Schulman: Humans retain advantages in judgment, self-checking, and the ability to navigate the weak points of a system. Each new model closes some gaps, but users often experience a familiar cycle: a model initially looks extraordinary, then its shortcomings become apparent in sustained use. Coding output alone does not translate directly into a hundredfold productivity increase when the work remains bottlenecked by verification, judgment, coordination, and experimentation.

Charlie O’Neill: Another uncertainty is the distance between the present transformer-plus-reinforcement-learning recipe and the best learning system that could be built on available hardware. Progress may require an additional discontinuity, just as earlier scaling progress depended on innovations rather than a single unbroken recipe. If the necessary breakthrough is far from what current systems can discover, capabilities could asymptote instead of triggering rapid self-improvement.

Recursive self-improvement and research bottlenecks

Dwarkesh Patel: The counterargument is that once AI becomes even slightly better than the best human researchers at AI work, enormous parallelism and faster hardware could overwhelm other bottlenecks. The chess analogy is instructive: a roughly linear increase in skill can produce a sharp practical transition when a system crosses the human range. A modest advantage in research, replicated at very large scale, could have discontinuous consequences.

The panel distinguishes improvements that extend the existing paradigm from a replacement of the paradigm itself. If progress since 2012 can continue through further cumulative innovations, systems may eventually dominate human research and development. If it requires discarding core assumptions such as today’s architecture or optimization methods, merely running more current models may not be enough.

The participants agree that faster experimentation is not identical to autonomous scientific insight. Research involves choosing objectives, interpreting surprising results, and deciding which experiments deserve scarce resources. Still, systems that can run a few experimental loops, analyze outcomes, and select a sensible next experiment would already provide a large leverage point for AI labs.

Generalization, objectives, and scientific discovery

John Schulman: Some of the most important advances involve generalization that was hard to predict in advance. Pre-training on next-token prediction produced capabilities that early researchers did not necessarily expect, and post-training benchmarks do not always align with what users value. The panel therefore resists assuming that a clean objective in a training environment captures every kind of scientific breakthrough.

Beren Millidge: There is a difference between optimizing a well-specified objective and doing open-ended science. In an autoresearch-style setting, one can define a reward and improve it through repeated trials. Paradigm shifts may be different: neither people nor models may know how to specify the objective that would reveal the next major idea. Better thinking can update beliefs using existing evidence, but it cannot create new evidence on its own.

Dwarkesh Patel: On the other hand, AI could use vast amounts of computation to think through experiments before they are run and to analyze results afterward. With enough well-defined data and objectives, it might catch mistakes, propose ablations, or develop theory that shortens a research cycle. The question is whether those gains transfer from tightly verifiable tasks to the more open-ended work required for scientific and architectural breakthroughs.

Environments, domain training, and learning from deployment

The discussion turns to why labs are building reinforcement-learning environments for coding, finance, spreadsheets, presentations, and other knowledge-work domains. One explanation is commercial: these are valuable tasks that can fund further training. Another is that domain-specific practice can bake useful intuitions into model weights, making deployment cheaper and more reliable even if a sufficiently capable model could theoretically learn the domain on the fly.

John Schulman: Training across many domains may also transfer useful meta-skills. A model can learn how to identify relevant information, exercise taste, manage long-horizon tasks, and use tools. Direct data for recursive self-improvement is scarce and expensive to create, so broad task training can provide useful substrate alongside its commercial value.

Charlie O’Neill: The current sim-to-real approach is powerful but limited. Many real tasks, especially those requiring live interaction with people, are hard to reproduce in a data center. Simulation is necessary while sample efficiency is low, because no one can provide thousands of live human interactions for every training iteration. If efficiency improves, learning from deployment and off-policy traces may become more important, though that still raises questions about feedback quality and safe evaluation.

Data, architecture, parameters, and scaling laws

The panel argues that architecture and data cannot be reduced to a single percentage improvement. Architectural changes can unlock a qualitatively different regime. For example, efficient attention mechanisms can make very long contexts economical enough to train and use; without them, the relevant long-context data may be inaccessible in practice. At the same time, mid-training and post-training data often becomes useful only when models are large enough to exploit it.

As training becomes more reinforcement-learning-heavy, inference cost and rollout horizon become major design constraints. Frontier models may not simply grow in active parameters as quickly as public forecasts imply, because a model must be large enough for the hardest environments while still cheap enough to run repeatedly. The limiting factor may become the complexity and quality of available environments rather than raw parameter count.

The participants also discuss sparsity, data efficiency, and the lack of a complete theory of scaling laws. Sparse models separate total parameters from active parameters, but it is unclear how far sparsity can increase without tradeoffs in learning efficiency. With high-quality pre-training data becoming scarce, the best design may increasingly optimize for data efficiency rather than only compute efficiency.

Forecasts for remote work, research acceleration, and ASI

Asked when an AI could function as a drop-in remote worker across white-collar tasks over a month, the answers range from roughly a year for useful constrained versions to several years for full generality. The panel notes that organizations will adapt their tools and processes to make AI use easier, so practical adoption can arrive before systems handle every messy edge case. Long-tail tasks involving sustained context, interpersonal pressure, or novel organizational situations remain difficult.

The speakers caution that the quality of human remote work is itself highly variable. Existing systems can already complete substantial computer-use tasks, such as gathering documents through many websites, but this does not settle whether they can reliably manage complex projects, learn on the job, and respond well to prolonged feedback.

For a tenfold acceleration of AI research, estimates are more cautious: perhaps around two years for important experimental loops, with some participants preferring a longer horizon. The crux is whether a system can absorb information, update its judgment, plan the next experiment, and carry out multiple iterations without derailing. If that happens, faster AI research could accelerate the arrival of still greater capability.

On an AI that beats top human experts across all computer-based cognitive work, estimates range from roughly three or four years to five or ten years. The disagreement centers on long-horizon learning, memory, unfamiliar domains, and the long tail of expertise that has not yet received concentrated training. The closing view is not a single timeline but a shared recognition that automating AI research is unusually consequential: if systems can reliably improve the process that creates them, progress may become limited by hardware, experiments, institutions, and the remaining tasks that resist clean evaluation.
aiSummary: Dwarkesh Patel、Beren Millidge、John Schulman 与 Charlie O’Neill 讨论扩展、强化学习和研究自动化能否带来递归自我改进，并拆解可能阻断它的泛化、评估和现实学习瓶颈。
oneSentenceSummary: Dwarkesh Patel、Beren Millidge、John Schulman 与 Charlie O’Neill 讨论扩展、强化学习和研究自动化能否带来递归自我改进，并拆解可能阻断它的泛化、评估和现实学习瓶颈。
summary: 这场圆桌将递归自我改进视为一个有条件的系统问题，而不是对当前基准成绩的简单外推。嘉宾们对比了两条路径：一条是略强于顶尖人类研究者的 AI 能以大规模复制来缩短实验周期，另一条则受限于泛化、持续学习、验证、协作，以及可能需要新学习范式的现实。对话区分了目标明确环境中的优化与开放式科学，后者往往连目标和证据都尚未具备。随后讨论把 RL 环境、仿真、部署轨迹、架构、数据效率、稀疏性、推理成本和 rollout 时长，联系到加速研究的可行性。对于远程工作、十倍研究加速和广泛认知超越的时间预测仍明显分歧，因为长程判断与陌生场景中的学习依然没有定论。

mainPoints.point: 小幅研究优势可能在规模化后出现非连续变化
mainPoints.explanation: 乐观情形并非认为当前每一点基准提升都会自动复利，而是 AI 一旦略胜顶尖研究者，就可能被大规模并行复制，并以快于人类组织响应速度的方式缩短实验周期。

mainPoints.point: 开放式科学比优化明确奖励更困难
mainPoints.explanation: 嘉宾区分了具备可测目标的自动研究循环与范式转变：后者要求研究者先决定什么值得追求、解释意外结果，并取得新证据，之后才可能写出有用的目标。

mainPoints.point: 泛化和现实反馈仍是关键瓶颈
mainPoints.explanation: 当样本效率较低时，仿真可以支撑反复训练，但人际与组织任务很难在数据中心复现；未来从部署中学习或许有帮助，却也会带来反馈质量和安全评估问题。

mainPoints.point: 架构、数据和推理经济性共同限制下一阶段
mainPoints.explanation: 高效注意力、数据质量、稀疏性、活跃参数成本与 rollout 时长彼此牵连，因此更大的模型在高要求环境中需要反复行动时，并不会天然成为更便宜或更强的研究工作者。

keyQuotes: 当工作仍受验证、判断、协作和实验制约时，代码输出本身并不会直接转化为百倍生产率提升。
更好的思考可以利用现有证据更新信念，但不能自行创造新证据。
限制因素可能会变成可用环境的复杂度和质量，而不是原始参数量。
分歧集中在长程学习、记忆、陌生领域，以及尚未得到集中训练的长尾专业能力上。
